Open this QMD in RStudio. **Each numbered code chunk runs independently in a
fresh R session.** No downloaded data, packages beyond base R, or helper files
are needed. Start with the experiment and the target, predict the result,
then run the code. All data here are simulated or hypothetical.

**Main seminar:** Demos 1-4 prepare for B3. **Optional extension:** Demos 5-7
cover estimated variance and studentization; save them for later if needed.

## 1. One estimate per study

For a simple model inspired by the turnout example, imagine two independent
samples of 200 voters, with turnout probabilities 0.378 and 0.315. This is
not a reconstruction of the original experiment's assignment design or SEs.
The true difference is 0.063, or 6.3 percentage points.

**Predict:** Will every estimate equal the truth? What should its average be?

```{r}
#| label: demo-1-repeated-studies
set.seed(210071)
B <- 10000
n_per_group <- 200
p1 <- .378
p0 <- .315
truth <- p1 - p0
estimates <- replicate(B, {
  y1 <- rbinom(n_per_group, size = 1, prob = p1)
  y0 <- rbinom(n_per_group, size = 1, prob = p0)
  mean(y1) - mean(y0)
})
c(truth = truth,
  average_estimate = mean(estimates),
  bias = mean(estimates) - truth,
  sampling_sd = sd(estimates),
  theoretical_se = sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n_per_group +
                         p0 * (1 - p0) / n_per_group),
  mse = mean((estimates - truth)^2),
  within_one_pp = mean(abs(estimates - truth) <= .01))
hist(100 * estimates, breaks = 30, freq = FALSE,
     col = "#D4E7EF", border = "white",
     xlab = "Difference in turnout (percentage points)",
     main = "One difference in means per simulated study")
abline(v = 100 * truth, col = "#B04C3E", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

**Pause:** Change `n_per_group` to 800, leaving B fixed. Then restore n and
change B. Which change affects the estimator's actual sampling distribution?
The one-point tolerance is `.01` because this code uses proportions.

## 2. Unbiasedness versus consistency

Here observations are IID Normal with mean 5 and SD 2. Compare the sample mean,
the first observation, and the sample mean plus 2. The last estimator is
deliberately flawed; it makes the distinction visible.

```{r}
#| label: demo-2-consistency
set.seed(210074)
B <- 10000
mu <- 5
sigma <- 2
sizes <- c(4, 16, 64)
results <- lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  estimates <- replicate(B, {
    x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
    c(Mean = mean(x), First = x[1], Shifted_mean = mean(x) + 2)
  })
  data.frame(n = n, estimator = rownames(estimates),
             average = rowMeans(estimates),
             sampling_sd = apply(estimates, 1, sd),
             bias = rowMeans(estimates) - mu,
             mse = rowMeans((estimates - mu)^2),
             within_one = rowMeans(abs(estimates - mu) <= 1),
             row.names = NULL)
})
do.call(rbind, results)
```

Which estimator remains centered at 5 but does not concentrate?
Which becomes precise about the wrong value? Simulation illustrates this;
the expectation and variance formulas establish the claims.

## 3. Potential outcomes and every possible assignment

This **four-unit** example is different from B3. Outcomes are hypothetical
percentages. We know both potential outcomes only because we invented the
population. Fix these four units and randomly assign exactly two to treatment.

```{r}
#| label: demo-3-potential-outcomes
y0 <- c(10, 20, 15, 25)
y1 <- c(15, 22, 21, 25)
truth <- mean(y1 - y0)
diff_means <- function(y, D) mean(y[D == 1]) - mean(y[D == 0])
D <- as.integer((1:4) %in% c(1, 3))
y <- ifelse(D == 1, y1, y0)
data.frame(unit = 1:4, y0, y1, effect = y1 - y0, D, observed = y)
c(ATE = truth, this_estimate = diff_means(y, D))

# Each COLUMN is one possible treated pair. All six are equally likely.
assignments <- combn(1:4, 2)
assignments
estimates <- apply(assignments, 2, function(treated) {
  D <- as.integer((1:4) %in% treated)
  y <- ifelse(D == 1, y1, y0)
  diff_means(y, D)
})
data.frame(treated = apply(assignments, 2, paste, collapse = ", "), estimates)
c(exact_expectation = mean(estimates), truth = truth,
  exact_bias = mean(estimates) - truth)

# Now the original pair ALWAYS selects treatment: no averaging over assignments.
selected_difference <- diff_means(y, D)
ATT <- mean((y1 - y0)[D == 1])
baseline_selection <- mean(y0[D == 1]) - mean(y0[D == 0])
c(observed_comparison = selected_difference,
  ATT = ATT, baseline_selection = baseline_selection,
  ATT_plus_selection = ATT + baseline_selection,
  ATE = truth, gap_from_ATE = selected_difference - truth)
```

The temporary `D` and `y` inside the function belong to that calculation;
the original four-unit assignment remains available outside it. The observed
comparison is not the treated group's average individual effect, nor is that
treated effect necessarily the ATE. This is a useful place to do the
add-and-subtract derivation on the board.

## 4. Reading concentration and simulation summaries

This final illustration directly simulates **estimators**, not raw outcomes.
Both sampling SDs shrink, but one estimator targets the wrong value. These
Normal distributions are invented to make CDF concentration easy to see;
they are not assumptions about B3's village estimator.

```{r}
#| label: demo-4-cdf-and-summaries
set.seed(210076)
B <- 10000
truth <- 2
sizes <- c(10, 50, 250)
summary_rows <- list()
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (j in seq_along(sizes)) {
  n <- sizes[j]
  accurate <- rnorm(B, mean = truth, sd = 3 / sqrt(n))
  shifted <- rnorm(B, mean = truth + 2, sd = 3 / sqrt(n))
  plot(ecdf(accurate), do.points = FALSE, verticals = TRUE,
       col = "#176B87", lwd = 2, xlim = c(-1, 7),
       main = paste("n =", n), xlab = "Estimate", ylab = "CDF")
  lines(ecdf(shifted), do.points = FALSE, verticals = TRUE,
        col = "#B04C3E", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  abline(v = truth, lty = 3)
  if (j == 1) legend("topleft", c("Centered at truth", "Centered at 4"),
                     col = c("#176B87", "#B04C3E"), lty = 1:2, bty = "n", cex = .8)
  for (design in c("accurate", "shifted")) {
    estimates <- if (design == "accurate") accurate else shifted
    summary_rows[[length(summary_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      n = n, design = design, mean = mean(estimates),
      bias = mean(estimates) - truth,
      sampling_sd = sd(estimates),
      mse = mean((estimates - truth)^2),
      within_one = mean(abs(estimates - truth) <= 1),
      mcse_of_simulated_mean = sd(estimates) / sqrt(B))
  }
}
par(old)
do.call(rbind, summary_rows)
```

The Monte Carlo SE describes precision in our **simulation of the estimator's
mean**. It is not the estimator's sampling SD. Use `sd(estimates)` for the
latter. `sd()` uses B − 1, so the numerical identity with simulation MSE is
exact when variance is instead calculated as
`mean((estimates - mean(estimates))^2)`; the difference is tiny at large B.

## 5. Optional: a biased but consistent variance estimator

We compare the squared deviations divided by n with R's `var()`, which
divides by n − 1. Both settle around the population variance, but only the
latter is unbiased. The SD itself need not be unbiased.

```{r}
#| label: demo-5-variance
set.seed(210075)
B <- 10000
sigma <- 2
results <- lapply(c(5, 30, 100), function(n) {
  estimates <- replicate(B, {
    x <- rnorm(n, mean = 5, sd = sigma)
    c(divide_by_n = mean((x - mean(x))^2),
      divide_by_n_minus_1 = var(x))
  })
  data.frame(n = n, estimator = rownames(estimates),
             truth = sigma^2,
             expected = c((n - 1) / n * sigma^2, sigma^2),
             simulated_average = rowMeans(estimates),
             sampling_sd = apply(estimates, 1, sd), row.names = NULL)
})
do.call(rbind, results)
```

## 6. Optional: Normal observations and an exact t distribution

Each simulated study calculates the mean and SD from the **same** sample.
For IID Normal observations, the resulting statistic has an exact
$t_{n-1}$ distribution. The empirical CDF only approximates that distribution.

```{r}
#| label: demo-6-normal-t
set.seed(210072)
B <- 20000
mu <- 5
sigma <- 5
sizes <- c(5, 30, 100)
t_values <- lapply(sizes, function(n) replicate(B, {
  x <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  (mean(x) - mu) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n))
}))
grid <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (j in seq_along(sizes)) {
  n <- sizes[j]
  plot(grid, ecdf(t_values[[j]])(grid), type = "l", lwd = 2,
       col = "#176B87", ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Studentized mean",
       ylab = "CDF", main = paste("n =", n))
  lines(grid, pt(grid, df = n - 1), col = "#B04C3E", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  lines(grid, pnorm(grid), col = "#957000", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
  if (j == 1) legend("topleft", c("Simulation", "t", "N(0, 1)"),
                     col = c("#176B87", "#B04C3E", "#957000"),
                     lty = 1:3, bty = "n", cex = .8)
}
par(old)
data.frame(n = sizes,
           left_sim = sapply(t_values, function(z) mean(z < -2)),
           right_sim = sapply(t_values, function(z) mean(z > 2)),
           each_t_tail = pt(-2, df = sizes - 1),
           each_Normal_tail = pnorm(-2))
```

`ecdf(t_values[[j]])` constructs a function. Applying it to `grid` evaluates
the fraction of simulated statistics less than or equal to each grid point.
The grid is for drawing curves; the full simulated vector is used for tail
probabilities, including values beyond the displayed range.

## 7. Optional: Exponential observations and the t reference

Keep mean = 5 and SD = 5 but use a strongly right-skewed population.
For an Exponential, both moments equal `1 / rate`. The simulation is otherwise
the same. Look at the **two separate tails**, not just their sum.

```{r}
#| label: demo-7-exponential-t
set.seed(210073)
B <- 20000
mu <- 5
sizes <- c(5, 30, 100)
t_values <- lapply(sizes, function(n) replicate(B, {
  x <- rexp(n, rate = 1 / mu)
  (mean(x) - mu) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n))
}))
grid <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 1000)
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (j in seq_along(sizes)) {
  n <- sizes[j]
  plot(grid, ecdf(t_values[[j]])(grid), type = "l", lwd = 2,
       col = "#176B87", ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Studentized mean",
       ylab = "CDF", main = paste("n =", n))
  lines(grid, pt(grid, df = n - 1), col = "#B04C3E", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  lines(grid, pnorm(grid), col = "#957000", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
  if (j == 1) legend("topleft", c("Simulation", "t reference", "N(0, 1)"),
                     col = c("#176B87", "#B04C3E", "#957000"),
                     lty = 1:3, bty = "n", cex = .8)
}
par(old)
data.frame(n = sizes,
           left_sim = sapply(t_values, function(z) mean(z < -2)),
           right_sim = sapply(t_values, function(z) mean(z > 2)),
           each_t_tail = pt(-2, df = sizes - 1),
           each_Normal_tail = pnorm(-2))
```

**Discuss:** A small sample containing mostly small observations can produce
both a low sample mean and a small sample SD. This can create a large negative
ratio. The exact Normal-sampling independence result does not carry over.
Finite positive variance still supports the CLT and the large-n studentized
Normal limit. Do not interpret the t reference as an exact result here.

[Estimation and Inference slides](https://www.mattblackwell.org/files/teaching/gov2000/s05-estimation-inference-slides-print.pdf),
Sections 1-2, with permission. Potential-outcomes framing follows Gerber and
